documentation.range: This species is endemic to Mexico, where its range extends from north to south) through the states Sinaloa, Durango, Zacatecas, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero, México, Morelos, Puebla y Oaxaca (Ávila-Villegas 2007, Domínguez-Vega et al. 2012, García-Vázquez et al. 2009, Muñiz-Martínez and Rojas-Pérez 2009, Reiserer et al. 2013). The elevational range extends from near sea level to 1,529 m (Wilson et al. 2010), although it has been recorded in pine-oak woodlands at least as high as 1,861 m asl (Monroy-Vilchis et al. 2005). Following taxonomic changes, range limits relative to both the northern Rio Fuente Beaded Lizard and southern Chiapan Beaded Lizard require further study (Reiserer et al. 2013). Within this wide area it is largely associated with patchily distributed seasonally dry deciduous forest (Reiserer et al. 2013).
documentation.population: This species occurs at low population densities, and beaded lizards are generally considered to be "relatively uncommon" (Campbell and Vannini 1988, Beck 2005). Between July 1986 and March 1989, Beck and Lowe (1991) captured and radio-tracked 15 individuals - including both adults and juveniles - of Heloderma horridum in an area of approximately 36 ha in Jalisco State. It is an uncommon species, and is hard to observe even by local people (Dominguez-Vega et al. 2017). Studies of wild populations are scarce probably due to the high search effort needed to locate individuals (H. Domínguez-Vega pers. comm. 2021). In an indirect study to analyze the observation frequency and hunting of wild populations of beaded lizards Domínguez-Vega et al. (2017), reported 187 sightings in five localities where this beaded lizard occurs.  Presumably the population is declining at a slow rate, though supporting documentation is lacking.
documentation.habitats:
Beaded lizards exhibit a close association with tropical deciduous tropical forests (Domínguez-Vega et al. 2012, Reiserer et al. 2013). Although this species has been recorded from pine-oak woodland and thorn scrub adjacent to dry forest, its use if these habitats is thought to be uncommon (Reiserer et al. 2013) and sighting records reported by Domínguez-Vega et al. (2017) suggest a preference for well-preserved tropical forest. It has been encountered in a variety of other habitats including livestock areas, mango orchards, garbage dumps and even urban areas (H. Domínguez-Vega pers. obs.).

It is semi-arboreal and most commonly encountered after summer rain (Beck and Lowe 1991). Despite these lizards' high public profile both locally and internationally, their ecology remains poorly-known largely because they spend much of their lives hidden in shelters (Beck and Lowe 1991). This species' ecology was studied by Beck and Lowe (1991), who found that shelters are generally abandoned burrows 1-2 m deep on slopes or the forest floor, but the species also shelters in trees. Animals move between shelters during their surface-active period, and at these authors' study site remained active for over eight months between early April and mid-November with activity temperatures between 22.6-36 °C. In Jalisco, beaded lizards show significant changes from the dry season to wet season in their activity temperatures (being active at cooler temperatures during wet season), timing of emergence (bimodal during dry season), and the amount of time spent on the surface (which is greater during the wet season) (Beck and Lowe 1991, Holcomb 2017).

The diet consists of reptile eggs (particularly those of spiny-tailed iguanas, Ctenosaura, whose nesting season coincides with a peak in beaded lizard activity at a Jalisco study site, and the eggs and nestlings of birds generally or exclusively taken from nests (Beck and Lowe 1991). Feeding on nesting mammals and the ingestion of beetle larvae 20-30 mm long have also been reported (Beck and Lowe 1991, Beck 2005). Home ranges of five Heloderma horridum individuals were found to average 21.6 ha, with substantial overlap (Beck and Lowe 1991). Animals in this study used both deciduous and semi-deciduous riparian forest habitats. Trees were more commonly used as shelters during the wet season (July to October).

Examination of reproductive tissues from road-killed specimens collected in Sonora, Jalisco, and Colima, Mexico (Goldberg and Beck 2001) shows that for both the Rio Fuerte and Mexican beaded lizards sperm formation (spermiogenesis) begins in late August and continues through at least early October. Male combat and mating occur in the autumn (September-October), clutches of 2-10 eggs are laid between October and December, and hatchlings emerge in July with the onset of the summer rains (Álvarez del Toro 1982, Beck and Ramírez-Bautista 1991, Beck 2005, Gienger et al. 2005).
documentation.threats: Although human envenomation is extremely rare (García-Grajales et al. 2020), beaded lizards are venomous and frequently subject to targeted persecution (often referred to as aversive hunting) by local people (Beck 2005). Domínguez-Vega et al. (2017) reported that almost 50% of sighting observations by local people they questioned where taking during hunts. The seasonally dry forests in which the species occurs are the most threatened biome in Mesoamerica, with the primary drivers being forest clearance for agriculture, cattle ranching and human population growth (Reiserer et al. 2013 and references therein). These impacts are exacerbated by fire and drought, and predictive models of climate change impacts in this region suggest that the long-term persistence of seasonally dry forests is unlikely (Trejo and Dirzo 2000, Miles et al. 2006, Golicher et al. 2012).
documentation.measures: This species is protected by Mexican law under the category A (Threatened). Very few seasonally dry tropical forests in Mexico and Guatemala are protected, which may increase the vulnerability of the species to land use change (Reiserer et al. 2013). Research is needed to identify suitable areas of this habitat for the conservation of beaded lizards and to inform the creation of new protected areas (Reiserer et al. 2013). It is important that management of the forests includes scientifically-informed conservation management within a cohesive conservation plan (Douglas et al. 2010). An education strategy aimed at local people is needed to reduce aversive hunting practices (Domínguez-Vega et al. 2017). This species is listed in CITES Appendix II. Preliminary studies have identified conservation areas for beaded lizards (Domínguez-Vega et al. 2012), and Reiserer et al. (2013) recommend refinement of these incorporating improved habitat suitability modelling, and the development of conservation plans that incorporate modern understanding of the species' population status and ecological requirements (including monitoring sufficient to conduct population viability analysis). Research is needed to confirm that the current taxonomy of beaded lizards accurately reflects species boundaries (Reiserer et al. 2013).
documentation.use_trade: This species is found in the illegal pet trade both locally and internationally, the latter particularly in Japan, Europe, and the USA.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of the large extent of occurrence, and because while habitat loss is ongoing and the population is thought to be in decline due to both this and pressure from persecution, at a global scale there is no evidence that the rate of decline is sufficient to qualify for any of the threatened categories.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Reiserer et al. (2013) proposed recognizing the four established subspecies of Heloderma horridum as full species, as these are morphologically diagnosable and have been found to exhibit relatively high levels of genetic divergence. This latter observation was based on the results of Douglas et al. (2010), although those authors did not propose elevating these taxa to specific status. While Reiserer et al. (2013) caution that the morphological diagnoses of the former subspecies are "somewhat incomplete" and that further research is needed to confirm their species-level arrangement, the four-species approach is now widely accepted and is followed here. There has been an assumption that intergradation occurs between H. horridum and H. exasperatum along a north-south gradient, but no definitive evidence of this exists (Reiserer et al. 2013). Recent confirmation that H. alvarezi occurs as far north as Oaxaca (García-Grajales et al. 2020) suggests that a possible intergradation area may exist here.
